summary: A 1977 extension to FTP, called XRSQ and XRCP, for mailing the text of a message to several recipients at once on ITS FTP servers. It is far more efficient than sending the text again for each person.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 743 proposes an FTP extension for mailing one text to several recipients. It offers two sequences: list recipients before sending the text, or send the text before listing recipients.

subtitle: An FTP extension for sending one message text to several recipients.

tldr.problem: Sending the same message to several recipients with ordinary FTP mail requires transmitting the text separately for each recipient.
tldr.mechanism: XRSQ selects a recipients-first or text-first scheme, XRCP specifies recipients, and MAIL or MLFL supplies the message text.
tldr.outcome: The extension allows one text to be sent to multiple recipients using a scheme suited to the FTP server's mail-handling approach.

today: The unit records RFC 743's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The RFC describes an extension for multi-recipient mail through ITS FTP servers.

sections.title: Sending One Text to Several Recipients
sections.content:
The extension is intended for users of ITS FTP servers, where sending a message to multiple recipients by ordinary FTP would require sending the text again for each additional recipient. The RFC proposes XRSQ to select a scheme and XRCP to specify recipient names; the existing MAIL or MLFL command provides the text.

The two schemes put recipient specification and text transmission in different orders, because neither sequence is optimal for every server.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of resending the same text for each recipient, the extension lets the sender transmit the text once and identify several recipients.

sections.title: Recipients-First and Text-First
sections.content:
In the recipients-first scheme, XRSQ R selects the method, and XRCP commands add names to a server-side list. A MAIL or MLFL command with no recipient argument then sends the message to the stored recipients. The server clears the list after the transmission, whether the final reply reports success or failure.

In the text-first scheme, XRSQ T is followed by MAIL or MLFL with no argument to store the text. Later XRCP commands deliver that stored text to each named recipient, with a reply for each recipient. The text remains stored until another MAIL/MLFL or XRSQ resets or replaces it.
sections.plainLanguage: Recipients-first stores the names and then sends the text once to that list. Text-first stores the text and then delivers it as each recipient is specified.

sections.title: Selecting and Checking a Scheme
sections.content:
An XRSQ with no argument tests whether the extension is implemented and resets the server to the default state with no scheme selected. An XRSQ question mark requests the server's preferred scheme in a 215 reply. The sender may then select R or T; the server can reject a scheme it cannot use with reply 501.

The RFC says XRSQ always resets stored scheme state, even when it returns a refusal or preference. Ordinary MAIL or MLFL commands with a non-null argument also reset the extension state.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can test for support and ask which scheme the server prefers. Selecting a scheme or sending an ordinary addressed message also resets the extension's stored state.

sections.title: Why Servers Might Prefer Different Schemes
sections.content:
Recipients-first supports bulk mailing because the server can hand one message and its recipient list to a central mailer. Text-first suits servers that deliver directly and need to return an individual success or failure for each recipient.

The RFC cautions that clients should use XRSQ to test support before sending XRCP, since an unrecognized command and an unselected scheme can otherwise be difficult to distinguish.
sections.plainLanguage: A central mailer may prefer the recipient list first, while a server delivering directly may prefer to report results one recipient at a time. Clients should check that the extension is supported.

references.text: Harvey, B., One More Try on the FTP, RFC 691, cited for reply-code choices.
